title: Your king comes on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9)
hookLine: lowly and riding on a donkey: words the gospels saw on Palm Sunday

cards: Leaders arrive with motorcades and flashing lights, or a jet on the tarmac. In the ancient world, a conquering king rode in on a warhorse or stood in a chariot, soldiers marching behind and captives in chains.

The animal said everything: I won, and I can do it again. Now a different arrival: crowds, shouting, branches in the road, and at the center a man on a young donkey, his feet nearly scraping the ground.
Many churches remember that scene every year on Palm Sunday. But the picture was painted centuries earlier, in the same book as yesterday's vision.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass."
Ass is the old English word for a donkey. Zechariah announces a king, the trumpets are ready, and then he says lowly.
The Hebrew can also mean poor, or humbled: a king who is just and brings rescue, but comes without swagger. The next verse explains the donkey.
God says the chariot and the warhorse will be cut off, the battle bow broken, and this king will speak peace to the nations.

teach.h: A DONKEY: AN ANIMAL OF PEACE.
teach.b: A donkey is the animal of farmers and traders, of ordinary days: a peace animal. The king arrives disarmed on purpose.
Centuries later, the Gospels tell how Jesus sent two disciples to bring a donkey and rode it down the Mount of Olives into Jerusalem, as crowds spread cloaks and branches.
Matthew and John both quote Zechariah to explain it. One curious detail: Zechariah, like much Hebrew poetry, says the same thing twice, an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass.
Matthew's account has two animals, a donkey and her colt. Readers have discussed that for centuries.
Jews still read Zechariah's king as a hope for the future; Christians hear it fulfilled on Palm Sunday.

teach.h: LOWLY, AND RIDING UPON AN ASS.
teach.b: Either way the picture holds: power that chooses to come low.

how: On Palm Sunday, the Sunday before Easter, many churches hold processions with palm branches and read the Gospel of Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey, often alongside Zechariah 9:9.

o: lowly, poor or humbled, as the king comes
angry, ready to ride out to battle
royal, crowned and seated on a high throne

games.q: what's inside Zechariah 9 — tap the pairs.
p: cut off, in the next verse
an animal of peace and ordinary days
can also mean poor, or humbled

s: Zechariah pictures the king on a warhorse
he comes lowly, on a donkey, and the warhorse and chariot are cut off.
Zechariah's poetry names an ass and a colt, and Matthew has a donkey and her colt.
Jews and Christians read Zechariah 9:9 the same way
Jews still read it as a hope for the future; Christians hear it as fulfilled on Palm Sunday.

games.q: you're a king, just and bringing rescue, about to enter your capital. the crowds are waiting. how do you arrive?
games.why: Zechariah's king comes "lowly, and riding upon an ass," and speaks peace. the Gospels tell how Jesus rode a donkey into Jerusalem.

practice: Think of a place where you hold some power, a parent, a boss, the one with the car keys, and picture a moment coming up where you could choose the donkey over the warhorse: ask instead of order, listen before deciding, let someone else go first.
Lowly doesn't mean weak; Zechariah's king is still a king. If you pray, ask for that kind of strength; if not, picture yourself arriving gently.

wordCard.voice: Ani, Hebrew for lowly, poor or humbled: Zechariah's word for a just king arriving lowly, on the animal of peace, which the Gospels saw on Palm Sunday.

orig.note: Hebrew: lowly, poor, humbled. the word Zechariah uses for the king.

carryVoice: Your line: lowly, riding. A king, and still on a donkey. That's day four hundred ninety-five.
